Bhante, in 'web books thingsastheyare section0006 html 77c255' (web books thingsastheyare section0006 html 77c255), what is the core doctrinal teaching regarding '[Section: The Tracks of the Ox]'?

In this section from *web books thingsastheyare section0006 html 77c255*, the master explains: *"[Section: The Tracks of the Ox] An excerpt from a talk given July 6, 1982 …Whichever theme you focus on, be earnest with it, keeping mindfulness in constant touch with the work you are doing."*. From the perspective of the Four Noble Truths, suffering arises whenever the mind grasps at impermanent phenomena (*anicca*) as a reliable self (*atta*). It is like grasping a poisonous cobra by the tail: tempting and sleek from afar, but deadly the moment you grasp it. Release the tail and live in safety. In sitting meditation, how do we work with the body and breath when 'web books thingsastheyare section0006 html 77c255' advises: 'There is only one thing: the'?

The practical guidance given in *web books thingsastheyare section0006 html 77c255* instructs: *"There is only one thing: the word buddho blending step by step with your awareness."*. When you sit on the cushion, do not wage war against wandering thoughts. First ground attention in the physical posture—soften the belly, relax the face, and allow the breath to find its natural rhythm. When thoughts arise, notice the space around them rather than following the story. It is like still, flowing water (nam lai rin): awareness flows smoothly perceiving sights and sounds, while the heart inside remains utterly motionless. Rest the mind gently in the rhythm of each natural in-and-out breath.

What advice is given in 'web books thingsastheyare section0006 html 77c255' (web books thingsastheyare section0006 html 77c255) for overcoming habitual reactivity regarding: 'As the mind becomes more and'?

Addressing everyday distress, the text emphasizes: *"As the mind becomes more and more still, the buddho you are repeating will more and more blend into one with your awareness."*. When emotional turbulence or conflict flares, the ego habitually wants to blame external circumstances. The Forest masters remind us that outer events are merely triggers; the actual suffering is the inner contraction of resistance. Step back for a single conscious breath, recognize the tightness as impermanent, and respond with patient goodwill. It is like an old brass spittoon: people may spit into it or polish it, but it never gets angry or vain. It simply does its duty without ego. Meet daily challenges with a spacious, generous heart.
